content: The Antonine Plague, also referred to as the Plague of Galen, was an ancient pandemic that likely involved either smallpox or measles. It was introduced to the Roman Empire by soldiers returning from military campaigns in the Near East. This epidemic claimed the lives of two Roman emperors: Lucius Verus, who died in 169 CE, and his co-regent Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who ruled until 180 CE. The epidemic was named after Marcus Aurelius's family name, Antoninus. According to the Roman historian Dio Cassius, the disease re-emerged nine years later, causing up to 2,000 deaths per day in Rome, with mortality affecting approximately one-quarter of those infected. The total death toll is estimated to have reached five million. During the outbreak in 166 CE, the Greek physician and writer Galen left Rome for his home in Asia Minor but returned in 168 CE at the request of the two emperors. Galen's observations of the epidemic, recorded in his treatise Methodus Medendi, are brief. He described symptoms such as fever, diarrhea, pharyngeal inflammation, and a skin eruption that appeared on the ninth day of illness, which could be either dry or pustular. However, Galen's account does not provide sufficient detail to definitively identify the disease, though most scholars have diagnosed it as smallpox. The epidemic had profound social and political consequences across the Roman Empire. The Roman military campaign in the East, led by Emperor Verus, was significantly hindered by the disease, as large numbers of troops succumbed to the illness. The Spanish writer Paulus Orosius later noted that many towns and villages in Italy and the European provinces were completely depopulated. The epidemic spread northward to the Rhine, infecting Germanic and Gallic tribes outside the Empire's borders. These northern groups, who had been pressing southward in search of land, encountered weakened Roman forces unable to repel them due to the epidemic's toll. From 167 CE until his death, Marcus Aurelius personally commanded legions near the Danube, attempting with limited success to halt the advance of Germanic tribes across the river. A major offensive against the Marcomanni was delayed until 169 CE due to a shortage of imperial troops. During this time, Marcus Aurelius also composed his philosophical work Meditations, in which he reflected on the pestilence, stating that it was less deadly than falsehood, evil behavior, and ignorance. As he lay dying from the disease, Marcus Aurelius reportedly said, Weep not for me; think rather of the pestilence and the deaths of so many others. The Plague of Cyprian, which occurred between 251 and 266 CE, marked another devastating outbreak. At its peak, it was reported that 5,000 people per day were dying in Rome. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, described the plague's symptoms in his essay De Mortalitate (On Mortality). His biographer, Pontius the Deacon, noted that the plague in Carthage coincided with the Decian persecution, during which Christians were scapegoated, much like Jews during the Black Death in the 14th century. Fifty years later, the North African Christian convert Arnobius defended Christianity against pagan accusations related to the plague. Historian William McNeill has suggested that the Antonine Plague and the Plague of Cyprian were caused by two different diseases, one being smallpox and the other measles, though the order is uncertain. The severe impact of these plagues on the European population suggests that the people had no prior exposure or immunity to either disease.
